doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Arriving at Hamilton well read; the zero from Professor Rudd
summary: He came to Hamilton better read than most, his father's Freudian reading shaped him, and he got a zero on an early English exam.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: It must have prepared you pretty well for college studies?

Well it did. I was a very bad student. I mean I was goofing off, I was playing in the jazz band, I was drinking beer if I could ever put together ten cents for a beer I was running around and stuff. I managed to pass my courses by and large but yeah — although I didn’t realize it, I came to Hamilton better read than probably most of the kids. But also my father had been very involved in — he was an autodidact. He had run away from home when he was 16 from a good family up on Cohasset, Massachusetts. And he had run away. And so he never really finished high school. So he didn’t have a college, sort of a well-rounded as we’d say, college education. But what he did have was, he was very smart, and had intellectual curiosity. And he had gotten involved, he had had Freudian therapy in the 1930s, which he badly needed, and so he read a great deal of psychology. So by the time I went to college I also was somewhat versed in Freudian lore, hardly an authority on Freud mind you, but I mean these terms the unconscious and whatnot were all sort of stuff that I understood. And one of my first exams, Boba Rudd, the infamous Boba Rudd, English professor in my day, gave us an exam, a typical exam of the time, mentioning a couple of poems that we were supposed to have read and said please tell me what the intention of the poet was. And my response on the exam was we cannot know the intention of the poet because it’s in the unconscious. And he gave me a zero. So I stopped pulling that stuff on him.
You know on that kind of thing you’re either going to get an A or you’re going to get a zero.
